title: The City Falls
sum: On the ninth day of the fourth month of Zedekiah's eleventh year the wall is breached and the Babylonian chiefs take seats in the Middle Gate. Zedekiah and his soldiers slip out by night through the king's garden, but they are caught near Jericho. At Riblah the king of Babylon kills Zedekiah's sons in front of him and blinds him. Jerusalem's houses and walls are burned and torn down, the people still in the city are marched off, and the poorest are left behind with vineyards and fields.

Nebuchadnezzar then gives an order to protect Jeremiah, who is handed to Gedaliah. The chapter ends by going back in time to a promise made to Ebed-melech the Cushite while Jeremiah was still shut up in the courtyard of the guard. The king of Judah loses everything; the foreign court official who trusted God is told he will keep his life.
readings: Read as history

The chapter is a short account of the fall, close to 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 52, written to explain what happened to Jeremiah. It adds the names of the Babylonian officers and the order given about the prophet, and it leaves out the burning of the Temple.
Read as a story of two men

Zedekiah, who feared his own officials (38:19), sees his sons killed and loses his eyes. Ebed-melech, who risked his life for Jeremiah, is told he will walk away alive 'because you trusted in me.' The chapter holds the two side by side.
Read as a puzzle of editions

The Greek has no 39:4–13. If the shorter text is the older, the Masoretic edition expanded the story from Kings and Jeremiah 52; if the Hebrew is original, the Greek lost the passage by a copyist's jump. See the variants.

views.H: The Babylonian side of the story is partly confirmed: a tablet of 595 BC is generally identified with the Nabu-sharrussu-ukin who matches the Nebo-sarsekim, the Rab-saris, of 39:3. The numbers and dates match 2 Kings 25. The date of the fall is 586 BC on this site (587 for some scholars).
views.C: 39:4–13 is missing in the Greek and is nearly the same as 2 Kings 25:4–7 and Jeremiah 52:7–16. Scholars divide: some call it a later expansion of an original that went straight from 39:3 to 39:14, and others a passage the Greek's source lost by a copyist's jump from one 'king of Babylon' to the next. 39:15–18 is placed here though it belongs before the fall.
views.J: The breach, the burning and the exile are remembered in the three weeks of the fasts: the Seventeenth of Tammuz and the Ninth of Av (Mishnah Taanit 4:6). The rabbis' explanation of the different dates for the breach is in Bavli Taanit 28b.
views.X: Ebed-melech, the Cushite court official, can be set beside the Ethiopian court official who believed Philip's message (Acts 8:26-39). Both are foreigners from the upper Nile, and both serve a ruler.
views.F: Little in this chapter looks forward, except that the people left to farm are the first ones who will plant in the land again; see 40:10-12.

deep.h: Which witnesses stand behind these chapters
deep.b: For chapters 39–45 I read: the Leningrad Codex Hebrew text with its Ketiv and Qere marks (the base of the Plain); the Qumran scrolls 2QJer (2Q13) and 4QJer-d (4Q72a) in the transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook; and the Greek as printed by Swete from Codex Vaticanus. I did not read Ziegler's Göttingen text, the Targum, the Vulgate or the Peshitta; where this site says 'the Greek' for these chapters it means Swete's printed text, and the critical text may differ. 2QJer preserves only 42:7–14, 43:8–11 and parts of 44:1–14; 4QJer-d only 43:2–10. Most verses in these seven chapters have no scroll, and I say so in the variant entries where it matters.

The Greek is shorter than the Hebrew in all seven chapters, as it is across Jeremiah. Besides the missing verses 39:4–13, it lacks many small items: 'the LORD declares', titles such as 'the prophet', 'the chief of the guard' and 'king of Babylon' after a name, 'son of Shaphan', and 'disease' in the list 'sword, famine and disease'. I give a variant entry only where a clause with real content differs. Examples in this chapter are 39:1 and 39:4–13.

echoes: 2 Kings 25:1–12; Jeremiah 52:4–16; Ezekiel 12:1–16; Ezekiel 17:11–21; Jeremiah 34:1–7; Jeremiah 38:7–13; Jeremiah 21:9; Jeremiah 45:5; Acts 8:26–39

settings.by: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, through Nebuzaradan
settings.to: Nebuzaradan, the chief of the guard
settings.when: after the breach and burning of Jerusalem, in the summer of 586 BC, from Riblah
settings.why: To protect the prophet and give him a free choice of where to live. Jeremiah had urged Judah to submit to Babylon (27:12; 38:17).
views: Some see a reward for Jeremiah's message that Judah should serve Babylon; others a gesture to win the goodwill of those in Judah who favored Babylon; the book itself says only that Nebuchadnezzar gave the order.

settings.to: Ebed-melech the Cushite, a court official (38:7 gives him that rank) who had rescued Jeremiah from the cistern
settings.when: while Jeremiah was shut up in the courtyard of the guard, before the fall (the chapter places it after, as a flashback)
settings.why: To thank and protect the one man who had acted with courage for Jeremiah, in the same hour the city's leaders were to be destroyed. It makes an example of trust: a foreigner and a royal servant, not a prince, is promised his life.
settings.readers: Exiles who read the book after 586 saw a pattern: those who trusted God lived, though the kingdom did not. It prepares for the word to Baruch in 45:5.

title: Jeremiah and Gedaliah at Mizpah
sum: The chief of the guard finds Jeremiah in chains among the exiles at Ramah and sets him free. He says the LORD had warned of this calamity and that the people had brought it on themselves. Jeremiah may go to Babylon, where he will be looked after, or stay with Gedaliah at Mizpah. He stays.

Gedaliah, whom Babylon has put in charge, tells the scattered commanders and their men to settle, serve Babylon and gather the harvest. Judeans return from Moab, Ammon and Edom and bring in a great wine and fruit harvest. Then Johanan warns Gedaliah that Baalis of Ammon has sent Ishmael to kill him, and offers to kill Ishmael first. Gedaliah refuses and calls it a lie.
readings: Read as political history
After the fall Babylon chose a Judean of a loyal family to rule a small province from Mizpah, and the survivors rebuilt a farming life around him. The chapter shows how quickly it fell apart.
Read as a portrait of Jeremiah
Offered comfort at Babylon's court, Jeremiah stays with the poor and the leaderless. His choice matches his letter to the exiles (29:5-7): build and plant where you are.
Read as a tragedy of trust
Gedaliah's good faith toward everyone, including Ishmael, is both what makes him a good leader and what kills him.

views.H: Mizpah (probably Tell en-Nasbeh) had no burned layer in 586 and prospered in the sixth century. Seals and an Ammonite seal impression from Tell el-Umeiri fit the names here. The harvest mentioned shows the land was still able to produce.
views.C: 40:1-6 and 39:11-14 give two accounts of Jeremiah's release, which many take to come from different sources or stages. Gedaliah's speech (40:9-10) is nearly the same as 2 Kings 25:24; the Greek and 2 Kings read 'the Chaldeans' servants' where the Hebrew of Jeremiah reads 'from serving the Chaldeans' (see the variant).
views.J: Gedaliah's death is remembered in the Fast of Gedaliah on the third of Tishri, which the Talmud says is counted with the Temple's burning (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 18b).
views.X: No New Testament writer quotes this chapter. A reader's association, not a New Testament use of Jeremiah 40: Jesus' lament over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41-44) also grieves a city before its ruin.
views.F: Gedaliah's offer, 'serve the king of Babylon, and things will be good for you,' is close to Jeremiah's advice to the exiles (29:5-7); in the end it was not heeded.

deep.b: No Babylonian text calls Gedaliah a governor. The Hebrew says only that the king 'put him in charge' (40:5, 7). Some scholars treat Mizpah as the seat of a small province under Babylon; others as a local arrangement for the farming population. Either way, he is the only leader of the people in the land whom the Bible names between the fall and the return.

settings.what: The chief of the guard's speech to Jeremiah
settings.to: Jeremiah, in chains among the exiles at Ramah
settings.when: shortly after the city fell, as the captives were gathered to be marched to Babylon
settings.why: To set Jeremiah free and offer him a free choice. The speech explains the catastrophe as the LORD's doing for Judah's sin, which is Jeremiah's own message in the mouth of an enemy.
views: Either he knew Jeremiah's teaching, or the book's authors give Jeremiah's message to a foreigner so that even the victors confirm it.

settings.by: Gedaliah son of Ahikam, appointed by Babylon
settings.to: the commanders of the Judean forces and their men, who had come to Mizpah
settings.when: soon after he took office, before the harvest
settings.why: To persuade armed men who had held out against Babylon to put down their weapons, farm and trust him to speak for them to the Babylonian inspectors. He gives them an oath, which is how a ruler gave safety to a band that might otherwise raid.

settings.by: Johanan son of Kareah and the commanders; Gedaliah
settings.to: Gedaliah, and in private to him
settings.when: in the harvest season after the return of the refugees
settings.why: Johanan wants to stop a plot by killing the plotter first, quietly; Gedaliah will not kill a man on a rumor, and will not believe a royal prince would kill him. The exchange shows why Gedaliah's trust was both his virtue and his mistake.

title: The Murder of Gedaliah
sum: In the seventh month Ishmael, a prince of the royal family, comes to Mizpah with ten men. They eat a meal with Gedaliah, then get up and kill him, together with the Judeans and Babylonian soldiers there. On the second day, before anyone knows, eighty mourners come from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria bringing offerings for the ruined temple. Ishmael meets them weeping, invites them in, and kills all but ten, who buy their lives with hidden food. He throws the bodies into Asa's old cistern.

He takes the rest of the people captive and heads for Ammon. Johanan and the commanders catch up with him at the great pool of Gibeon. The captives run to Johanan, but Ishmael escapes with eight men. The survivors stop near Bethlehem, planning to flee to Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans.
readings: Read as political history
Ishmael, of David's line, kills Babylon's man at Mizpah, probably with the backing of Ammon. Judah's last government is destroyed, and Babylon is likely to retaliate; the refugees' fear is realistic.
Read as a story of betrayal
The murder happens at a table. Ishmael greets mourners with tears and then kills them. The story gives no motive beyond ambition, and ends with a man who got away.
Read as a turning point of the book
Everything before the fall was warning; here the last hope of a Judean community in the land is put out, and chapters 42–44 follow its journey away.

views.H: The names fit what we know: a royal prince, the king of Ammon, and the places Mizpah, Gibeon and Bethlehem. Excavation at Gibeon found the pool and a wine industry; Mizpah (Tell en-Nasbeh) shows no destruction layer in 586. The date of the murder is uncertain (see the note at 41:1).
views.C: 41:1-3 is told again in 2 Kings 25:25 in two lines. The Greek has no major gaps in this chapter, only small differences in names (for example 'Salem' for Shiloh).
views.J: The Fast of Gedaliah on the third of Tishri keeps the date. The Talmud says the death of the righteous is equated with the burning of the Temple (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 18b).
views.X: Matthew quotes Jeremiah 31:15, Rachel weeping at Ramah, for Herod's killing of the children (Matthew 2:18). Some readers link that verse to the Ramah of 40:1, the place where the captives were gathered.
views.F: No word of hope falls in this chapter, but 41:5 shows that people from the north still thought of the Temple's site as the LORD's house, which later hopes for rebuilding relied on.

deep.b: The text says only that Baalis sent Ishmael (40:14) and that Ishmael was of the royal line (41:1). Some scholars see a claim to David's throne, since Gedaliah was a commoner appointed by the enemy. Others see a plot by Ammon to weaken a rival province. Others note Ishmael did not stay: he took captives and ran to Ammon, which suggests he served another's plan. Josephus tells the story with added details (Antiquities 10.9), which are late and cannot be checked.

echoes: 2 Kings 25:25-26; Jeremiah 40:13-16; Psalm 41:9; 1 Kings 15:22; 2 Samuel 19:37-40; Zechariah 7:3-5; Zechariah 8:19

settings.to: eighty men from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria, in mourning and carrying grain offerings and frankincense for the house of the LORD
settings.when: on the second day after Gedaliah's murder, before anyone outside Mizpah knew of it (41:4)
settings.why: The eighty are pilgrims from the old northern kingdom who still treated the Temple's site as holy and came to give offerings there in grief. Ishmael meets them as a fellow mourner and brings them to Mizpah, where he kills all but ten, who offer their hidden stores of wheat, barley, oil and honey. The text gives no reason; readers suggest secrecy about the murder just done, or greed.
settings.readers: Exiles and later readers learned from this scene that the ruined Temple was still visited, and that Ishmael's murders went beyond a political killing.

title: Do Not Go to Egypt
sum: The commanders and all the people ask Jeremiah to pray for the remnant and to tell them where to go. They swear that they will obey the LORD whatever he says. After ten days the answer comes: if they stay in Judah, the LORD will build and plant them and will not tear them down, for he has changed his mind about the harm he did; they need not fear the king of Babylon, for he will save them. If they go to Egypt, the sword and famine they fear will follow them there, and they will die.

Jeremiah then tells them what they have done: they sent him to the LORD, promising to obey, and they already meant to disobey. He ends with a plain warning that they will die in the place where they want to live.
readings: Read as a final offer
The words of 1:10 are turned toward the future: build, plant, not demolish and pull up. The offer is real; it depends on the people.
Read as a test
The people ask for guidance already decided. Jeremiah's reply shows the request was not sincere, and 43:2-3 reveals they had made up their minds.
Read as covenant curse
Deuteronomy's last curse, a return to Egypt, becomes a threat. The Exodus is undone by the people who go back.

views.H: Egypt was the obvious refuge, close and in conflict with Babylon, and Judean communities in Egypt are attested for the next two centuries.
views.C: 42:7-22 is in the Deuteronomistic prose style, with its stock phrases (sword, famine and disease; curse, horror, cursing word, disgrace). 2QJer preserves 42:7-14 and agrees with the Masoretic Text in the places that matter. The Greek lacks 'disease' in 42:17 and 22 and has the LORD himself bring them back in 42:12.
views.J: The murder of Gedaliah, which set this flight in motion, is remembered in the Fast of Gedaliah on the third of Tishri (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 18b).
views.X: In Matthew 2:13-15 Joseph takes the infant Jesus to Egypt, a refuge of another kind (Matthew quotes Hosea 11:1 there, not Jeremiah). Paul's pair of building up and tearing down in 2 Corinthians 10:8 uses the same two ideas as Jeremiah's 'build and plant', as a parallel and not a quotation; 1 Corinthians 3:6-9 uses planting and building as a general picture of church work.
views.F: The conditional promise of building and planting (42:10) is the same promise made unconditionally to the restored people in 31:28 and 32:41.

deep.b: Jeremiah 18:7-10 says the LORD can change a decree if a nation responds. Chapter 42 is that rule at work on a small scale: 'If you will truly stay ... I will build you up.' The offer was refused, and the book then shows what happened. Jeremiah did not say 'this will happen'; he said 'if.' Readers who ask whether his prophecies were fulfilled need to ask which kind of prophecy each one was: a prediction, a warning with an if, or a promise.

echoes: Jeremiah 1:10; Jeremiah 18:7-10; Jeremiah 24:6; Jeremiah 31:28; Deuteronomy 17:16; Deuteronomy 28:68; Hosea 8:13; Isaiah 30:1-5; Matthew 2:13-15

settings.by: the commanders, Johanan, Jezaniah and all the people, 'from the smallest to the greatest'
settings.to: Jeremiah the prophet, at Geruth Kimham near Bethlehem
settings.when: after the murder of Gedaliah, before they had gone on to Egypt
settings.why: To ask Jeremiah to pray and to tell them where to go. They bind themselves with an oath to obey, which turns the answer into a test of whether they will keep it.

settings.what: The LORD's answer: stay, do not go to Egypt
settings.to: Johanan, the commanders and the whole remnant, called together by Jeremiah
settings.why: To give them the answer they asked for, with both sides of the choice: life in the land with the LORD's protection if they stay, death in Egypt if they go. It also tells them that the fear that drives them, of Babylon, has no ground if they trust him.
settings.readers: Exiles who read this later learned that the survivors in Egypt had been warned, and that a return to the land had been on offer.
views: Some think it was a real offer that the survivors refused; others that the book shapes Jeremiah's words so as to blame the people in Egypt and defend the exiles in Babylon as the true remnant (compare 24:5-10).

title: Tahpanhes
sum: When Jeremiah finishes, Azariah, Johanan and the other proud men call him a liar. They say the LORD did not send him and that Baruch has talked him into handing them over to Babylon. They disobey, take everyone, including Jeremiah and Baruch, and go to Egypt as far as Tahpanhes.

There the LORD tells Jeremiah to hide large stones in the brick terrace at the entrance of Pharaoh's house, in sight of the Judeans. He is to say that Nebuchadnezzar, the LORD's servant, will set his throne over these stones and spread his tent. He will strike Egypt, burn its temples, carry off its gods and smash the standing stones of the sun-city.
readings: Read as a prophet's sign-act
Like the loincloth (13) and the jar (19), the buried stones are a visible word: they are buried and then become a throne.
Read as history
Nebuchadnezzar did campaign against Egypt (568/567 BC), but no source says he took it or set up a throne at Tahpanhes. The prophecy and the facts are compared in the notes.
Read as a judgment on Egypt's gods
The oracle is aimed at the temples and pillars of Egypt as much as at its king; compare the oracles on Egypt in Jeremiah 46 and Ezekiel 29–32.

views.H: Tahpanhes was a frontier fortress; Petrie's dig at Tell Defenneh found a large building and a brick platform near it. There is no record of a Babylonian throne there.
views.C: 4QJer-d agrees with the Greek's shorter text in 43:6 and differs from both in 43:9; 2QJer has 'my servant' in 43:10 where the Greek has none. The chapter is a good case of the texts disagreeing on small things and agreeing on the whole. The Greek reads Heliopolis for Beth-shemesh and 'weapons' for the tent.
views.J: The Fast of Gedaliah remembers the murder that sent the remnant on this road to Egypt (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 18b).
views.X: Egypt appears again in the New Testament as a refuge, for the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:13-15).
views.F: Some readers hold that the prophecy was fulfilled only in part and that the full conquest of Egypt lies ahead; others see its full sense in the Persian conquest of 525 BC.

deep.h: Nebuchadnezzar and Egypt in the record
deep.b: Ezekiel dated a promise of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar to 571 BC (Ezekiel 29:17-20). A Babylonian fragment (BM 33041) says that in his thirty-seventh year he marched against Egypt and that Amasis called out his army, but the text breaks off. Josephus puts a conquest in the twenty-third year (Antiquities 10.180-182 (10.9.7 in Whiston's numbering)), unsupported by earlier sources. No source describes a Babylonian throne at Tahpanhes. Readers who hold that Jeremiah spoke detailed predictions must either reckon the raid of 568/567 as the fulfillment, or take the picture as a figure for Babylon's reach; those who see the prophets as warning in images do not expect a literal throne.

echoes: Jeremiah 13:1-11; Jeremiah 19:1-13; Jeremiah 25:9; Jeremiah 27:6; Jeremiah 46:13-26; Ezekiel 29:17-20; Ezekiel 30:10-19; Genesis 41:45; Isaiah 19:18; Jeremiah 15:2

settings.what: The accusation against Jeremiah and Baruch
settings.by: Azariah son of Hoshaiah, Johanan son of Kareah and 'the arrogant men'
settings.to: Jeremiah, in front of all the people at the end of his speech
settings.when: just after he told them not to go to Egypt
settings.why: To reject the answer and blame the messenger, naming Baruch as the one behind it, so that disobedience looks like loyalty.

settings.by: the LORD, through Jeremiah, with an acted sign
settings.to: the Judeans who watched at the entrance of Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes
settings.when: soon after the refugees arrived in Egypt, about 586 BC if the flight followed Gedaliah's murder that autumn, or about 582 BC if the murder is dated later, to the year of the deportation in Jeremiah 52:30 (see the note at 41:1)
settings.why: To tell the refugees, with their eyes as well as their ears, that the king they fled would come to the place they thought safe. The hidden stones would become the base of his throne.
settings.readers: Judeans in Egypt and in Babylon who read it later could see that Egypt, too, was not beyond the LORD's reach.

title: The Queen of Heaven
sum: Jeremiah speaks to all the Judeans living in Egypt, from Migdol to Pathros. He reminds them of the ruins of Judah, which came because their ancestors burned incense to other gods. He warns that those who came to Egypt will die by sword and famine, and that only a few will return.

The men who know their wives burn incense, and the women, answer that they will not listen: they will go on burning incense to the Queen of Heaven, pouring drink offerings and baking cakes, as they and their ancestors did in Judah. They ate well then. Since they stopped, they say, they have lacked everything. Jeremiah replies that the LORD remembered the incense and the fall followed. He tells them to go ahead and keep their vows, swears that his name will not be used in Egypt, and gives a sign: Pharaoh Hophra will be handed over to his enemies.
readings: Read as a clash of two histories
The women read the past as prosperity under the goddess and disaster after her worship ended. Jeremiah reads the same past as warnings ignored and judgment come. Both claim the evidence.
Read as a picture of ordinary religion
The chapter is one of the few windows on the religion of families rather than priests and kings. Women, men, bread, vows, cakes and wine: not a state cult, but a household habit.
Read as the book's last word to the people
After this speech Jeremiah has no further address to a group. What follows is a private word to Baruch.

views.H: Elephantine papyri show a Judean garrison in Upper Egypt a century later with its own temple, and Kuntillet Ajrud and the Judean pillar figurines show goddess-worship in Israel and Judah earlier. Hophra (Apries) was overthrown by Amasis about 570 BC and died soon after.
views.C: The chapter is in the prose style linked with Deuteronomy, but the women's speech is vivid and unlike it. The Greek lacks Memphis in 44:1, has 'rulers' in 44:9, omits 'to shape her image' and 'mine or theirs'. 2QJer preserves 44:1-3 and 12-14 and has the full Hebrew triple (sword, famine, disease) at 44:13.
views.J: Radak takes the cakes as foods prepared for the Queen of Heaven (on 44:19). The Queen of Heaven is plainly an idol in the Jewish reading.
views.X: Christian readers have used the chapter against idolatry, and it is sometimes raised in debate over the title 'Queen of Heaven' for Mary. The card below sets out how the churches answer.
views.F: The few who return from Egypt (44:14, 28) are the seed of a later remnant, for those who read in Jeremiah a promise that God keeps some alive even in judgment; the oath 'As the LORD lives' is taken from Judeans in Egypt here, while 16:14-15 and 23:7-8 promise a new oath, sworn by the God who brings his people back from the north.

deep.b: Jeremiah 7:18 shows the cult at work in Judah: children gather wood, fathers light the fire, women knead dough for cakes. Jeremiah 44 gives the women's side. Outside the Bible, Mesopotamian texts call Ishtar 'queen of heaven' and offer her a kind of cake (kamanu); the Judean pillar figurines of the eighth and seventh centuries, many hundreds of them, show a female figure in homes and tombs; and Kuntillet Ajrud's inscriptions name Yahweh with 'his asherah'. Scholars such as Susan Ackerman, Mark Smith and William Dever use these facts to argue that goddess-worship was part of ordinary religion in Judah and that the prophets' campaign against it was a minority position. The prophets and the Deuteronomists say the opposite: the worship was a betrayal. The Bible's own historians agree that the cult existed; they differ with the women on what it meant.

Numbers 30 lets a husband cancel his wife's vow on the day he hears it, and holds her to it if he stays silent. The women's question, 'is it without our husbands?', answers an unspoken charge and claims their husbands consented. Jeremiah's reply in 44:25 is sarcastic: if the vows stand, let them stand. The rule in Numbers does not make the vow right, only binding on the woman.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Jeremiah answers the women with their own word 'remember'
deep.b: The women say 'we ... our ancestors ... our kings' did this and 'we saw no harm' (44:17). Jeremiah's reply (44:21) turns on the verb 'remember': 'was it not that incense the LORD remembered?' The Bible's verb for the LORD remembering a person is usually a promise (Genesis 8:1; Exodus 2:24). In 44:21 it is the reverse: a remembered offense. The repeated list of kings, officials and people of the land is plain in the text. The suggestion that the speech is built so that the women's boast of a shared tradition ('we and our ancestors') is answered by a shared memory ('you and your ancestors'), with the LORD as the one who keeps the record, is Claude's own reading of how the speech is put together. It is offered as a theory, not as a claim about history.

echoes: Jeremiah 7:16-20; Jeremiah 2:23-28; Jeremiah 16:14-15; Jeremiah 23:7-8; Jeremiah 1:11-12; Jeremiah 28:9; Deuteronomy 18:21-22; Numbers 30:6-15; 2 Kings 21:1-7; 2 Kings 23:4-14; Ezekiel 8:14; Isaiah 11:11

settings.what: Jeremiah's sermon to the Judeans in Egypt
settings.to: all the Judeans living in Egypt: at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis and in Pathros
settings.when: some time after the flight; no date is given. Some place it soon after 586, others a decade or more later, before Hophra's fall about 570 BC
settings.why: To tell the refugees that they are repeating the cause of the fall they saw. It ends on a note of judgment: no one will escape except a few fugitives.
settings.readers: Judeans in Egypt, Babylon and Judah who read the book after the fall could use it to see where the exile community in Egypt stood.
views: A great assembly (44:15), perhaps at a festival of the goddess or a harvest gathering, since all Pathros answers.

settings.by: all the men who knew their wives burned incense, all the women, and all the people
settings.when: at the same gathering, in answer to the sermon
settings.why: To reject Jeremiah's word outright and to defend their cult: it is a tradition of their ancestors and kings, and it brought prosperity. Their own claim shows the women as the ones who kept the cult.

settings.to: the men and the women who answered
settings.why: To reverse their reading of history: the troubles came because of the incense, not because it stopped.

settings.what: The last word: the LORD swears and gives a sign
settings.to: all Judah in Egypt, with the women singled out
settings.why: To answer the vow with an oath: the name of the LORD will not be used in Egypt, and the words he has spoken will stand. The sign is the downfall of Pharaoh Hophra, which the hearers could watch for.

traditions.q: Is it idolatry to call Mary 'Queen of Heaven'?
views: No. Mary is a creature, honored and not worshiped. The Catechism says she was taken up into heavenly glory and exalted by the Lord as Queen over all things (966, citing Lumen Gentium 59), and that devotion to her differs in kind from the adoration given to God (971). Pius XII set up the feast of her Queenship in 1954 (Ad Caeli Reginam). Teachers such as Scott Hahn root the title in the Davidic queen mother (1 Kings 2:19), not in the goddess of Jeremiah.

Orthodox hymns for the feast of the Dormition call Mary 'Queen' (the Lamentations for the Theotokos say heaven receives 'her Queen' and call her 'Sovereign Queen and Mother of God'), and honor her as Theotokos, 'God-bearer.'

The Lutheran confessions call Mary the blessed Virgin, 'most worthy of the most ample honors,' and hold her up as an example of faith (Apology XXI), but they reject praying to saints, because Scripture 'sets before us the one Christ as the Mediator' (Augsburg Confession XXI). They grant that the blessed Virgin and the saints may pray for the church in general, and they do not teach the title 'Queen of Heaven.'

Religious worship is to be given to God 'and to him alone; not to angels, saints, or any other creature,' and not 'in the mediation of any other but of Christ alone' (Westminster Confession 21.2). The Heidelberg Catechism, Q. 94, lists 'invocation of saints, or any other creatures' among the sins forbidden by the first commandment.

Article XXII of the Thirty-Nine Articles (titled 'Of Purgatory') calls 'the Romish Doctrine concerning Purgatory, Pardons, Worshipping, and Adoration, as well of Images as of Reliques, and also invocation of Saints' a 'fond thing vainly invented.' It does not mention Mary or the title. The Book of Common Prayer also keeps 'The Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary,' as the Church of England's website lists it.
The Second London Baptist Confession (1689) gives worship and prayer to God alone, and not to angels, saints or any other creature (22.2).

title: A Word for Baruch
sum: Chapter 45 is a short, private message to Baruch, dated to the fourth year of Jehoiakim (605/604 BC), the year he wrote down Jeremiah's words. Baruch had cried out in weariness: the LORD has added sorrow to his pain, and he is worn out with groaning and cannot find rest.

The LORD answers with what he is doing to the whole land: what he built he is demolishing, and what he planted he is pulling up. Baruch is not to look for great things for himself. Calamity is coming on everyone, but Baruch will have his life as loot wherever he goes.
readings: Read as a rebuke
Baruch wanted more than a scribe's lot, perhaps standing among the officials of Shaphan's circle, and is told to want less.
Read as comfort
The LORD hears Baruch's weariness and gives him what he can promise: his life, in every place.
Read as the book's seal
A word to the man who wrote the book ends the stories of Jeremiah's life, and matches the word to Ebed-melech (39:15-18).

views.H: Dated to 605/604, it belongs to the time of chapter 36, and is out of order in the book. The promise of life 'wherever you go' fits Baruch's journey to Egypt.
views.C: Some scholars take 45 as the closing note of the stories of 26–44, signed by Baruch (as author or as subject). In the Greek it stands as chapter 51:31-35, at the end of the narrative before the account of the fall (chapter 52), while the Hebrew places it before the oracles on the nations. The Greek lacks 'even this whole land' in 45:4.
views.J: Later writings put under Baruch's name, among them 2 Baruch, show him as a seer of the Temple's fall; none is in the Jewish canon.
views.X: The theme of seeking great things can be set beside the Gospels' teaching on greatness (Mark 10:35-45), as an association of this site and not a New Testament use of the chapter. The books Baruch (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox churches) and 2 Baruch (in no church's canon) were written in his name.
views.F: There is no promise of a restored kingdom here. The promise of life 'wherever you go' stands for any time of collapse.

deep.b: Chapter 45 is dated 20 years before the events of chapters 40–44. Three answers are common. It is Baruch's signature on the story he wrote (Jeremiah 36 tells how he wrote the first scroll; this is his own entry). It rounds off a frame: chapter 36 (the written word) and chapter 45 (the one who wrote it) enclose the stories. Or an editor placed it last, before the oracles on the nations, to end the story of the prophet on a promise: no one is promised anything in the book except life.

echoes: Jeremiah 36:1-8; Jeremiah 36:32; Jeremiah 39:15-18; Jeremiah 1:10; Jeremiah 42:10; Jeremiah 20:18; Jeremiah 8:18; Mark 10:35-45

settings.to: Baruch son of Neriah, the scribe who wrote out Jeremiah's words
settings.when: in the fourth year of Jehoiakim (605/604 BC), while Baruch was writing the scroll that Jehoiakim would burn (Jeremiah 36)
settings.why: To meet a scribe's complaint with the LORD's own plan: he is not building great things but watching them come down, and is to ask for nothing for himself. The promise of life is all he is given.
settings.readers: The exiles and later readers who read the book received it as the scribe's own place in the book: a man who gave his words to the work and received only his life.
views: Some think the chapter belongs to the time of chapter 36 and was placed here by the editors; others that Baruch's wish for 'great things' came later, in the troubles after the fall.
